cards.hook: The only reason to exercise a call early is the dividend.
cards.body: An American call on a non-dividend stock is never worth exercising early. Selling it always beats exercising, because you keep the remaining time value and defer paying the strike. The one exception is a dividend. When the payout exceeds the interest earned on the strike plus the call's remaining time value, exercising the day before the ex-date to capture the dividend can win. **Early exercise trades your time value for the dividend**, so it only pays when the dividend is bigger than what you surrender.
cards.depth: This is why deep-in-the-money calls on high-yield names get assigned early, and why short-call holders face assignment risk right before ex-date. Puts flip the logic: the interest saved by receiving the strike now makes early exercise of a deep put rational even with no dividend at all.

cards.hook: Pure AI output has no copyright. Your edits around it might.
cards.body: The US Copyright Office has held that material generated entirely from a prompt is not protectable, because a prompt does not give the human enough control over the expressive result. But a person who selects, arranges, and edits AI outputs can claim copyright in **those human-authored contributions**, not the raw generations. The registration has to disclaim the machine-made parts. So the protectable layer is the arrangement and the edits sitting on top, and that layer can be very thin.
cards.depth: Reported in the Office's 2025 copyrightability guidance and the earlier Zarya of the Dawn decision, where a comic's text and panel layout were protected but the Midjourney images were not. Practitioners overclaim here: telling a client they 'own the output' because they wrote a clever prompt is simply wrong.

cards.hook: Stop mid-sentence so restarting needs no decision.
cards.body: The hardest part of a task is the activation threshold: the cold start where you have to decide what to do and force yourself to begin. You can pre-load tomorrow's start by quitting today in the middle of something easy and concrete, a half-finished sentence or a test that is written but not run. Re-entry then asks for no decision, just finishing a line already in front of you. **Leave the task mid-motion, not at a clean stopping point.**
cards.depth: Two mechanisms stack. The unfinished action stays mentally active and slightly nags, which lowers the pull to walk away, and the concrete next move removes the executive-function cost of choosing what to do. Hemingway used it on purpose: stop when you still know exactly what happens next.

cards.hook: Look at your holdout twice and it becomes training data.
cards.body: A hold-out set gives an honest out-of-sample estimate exactly once. The moment you check it, see a bad result, and go back to tweak the strategy, that data has leaked into your design decisions. Every look after the first is contaminated, and your 'out-of-sample' Sharpe is now an in-sample number wearing a disguise. **The test set is a one-shot resource, not a dial you tune against.** Iterate on training data or a validation split, and touch the true hold-out last, only to report.
cards.depth: This is why published strategies decay after release: the whole community kept iterating against the same historical window. Walk-forward design helps by advancing the test period, but even that erodes if you re-run it repeatedly and keep only the parameter sets that happened to survive.

cards.hook: Recall it: why does a metric rot the moment you target it?
cards.body: You saw this a few days back. When a measure becomes a target, people optimize the proxy instead of the goal it stood for, so the correlation that made it useful quietly breaks. **The number keeps climbing while the thing you actually cared about stops moving.** In trading it shows up when you optimize a backtest statistic, Sharpe or win-rate, until you have maximized the number and hollowed out the edge it was supposed to represent. Its name: Goodhart's law.
cards.depth: The defense is to keep the real objective separate from the proxy you steer by, and to rotate or add proxies before they get gamed. A metric nobody is allowed to optimize against stays informative the longest, which is why some firms guard their true evaluation set.

cards.hook: Your call's delta isn't its odds of finishing in the money.
cards.body: Traders read a 0.30 delta as 'about a 30% chance this expires in the money.' It isn't. Delta approximates N(d1), while the risk-neutral probability of expiring in the money is N(d2), and **d2 sits a full sigma-root-t below d1**. That wedge widens with volatility and time, so on a long-dated or high-vol option the true odds of finishing ITM can run several points under the delta. Delta is a hedge ratio and a dollar sensitivity, not a likelihood. Size positions off delta-as-probability and you quietly overstate your own win rate.
cards.depth: The two even carry different drifts. Under the risk-neutral measure the underlying grows at r, and N(d2) prices that in, while N(d1) is an expectation weighted by the payoff itself. For puts the sign flips. It is the same reason the 'probability of profit' on a broker screen and the delta rarely agree.

cards.hook: Copyright won't protect a style. Trademark law might.
cards.body: Artists suing over models trained to mimic them keep losing the copyright argument, because **US copyright never protected artistic style**, only fixed expression. The live exposure is elsewhere. If a tool is marketed as making art 'in the style of [named living artist],' or outputs get passed off as that artist's, that can support Lanham Act false-endorsement and right-of-publicity claims. The recognized wrong is consumer confusion about source and endorsement, not imitation itself. Practitioners fixated on the copyright headline are watching the wrong courtroom.
cards.depth: This is why a prompt box that lets users type a living artist's name is riskier than the training run behind it. The training may be fair use; the name-as-a-feature is a false-association claim the provider chose to manufacture. The defense you build for one theory does nothing for the other.

cards.hook: Hyperfocus isn't extra focus. It's a failure to disengage.
cards.body: The same weak inhibition that makes a boring task hard to start makes an engaging one hard to stop. Hyperfocus feels like a superpower and is really **the brake failing in the other direction**: attention locks onto something rewarding and the switch that should pull you off it never fires. That is why you surface from a build at 1 a.m. having skipped dinner. The move is not willpower to quit. It is an external interrupt you cannot argue with, an alarm across the room, a hard-stop meeting, a person expecting you. You cannot self-interrupt, so outsource the interrupt.
cards.depth: It is the mirror image of the activation problem, same root: inhibition and executive control gate both starting and stopping. Calling it a disengagement failure instead of a gift is what makes you set the stop in advance, rather than trusting yourself to notice the clock mid-lock.

cards.hook: A single backtest tests your hindsight, not your strategy.
cards.body: Fitting parameters once over the whole history and admiring the equity curve measures how well you explained a past you already knew happened. **Walk-forward analysis** refits the model on a rolling in-sample window, then trades the next unseen slice, again and again, so the only P&L you keep is out-of-sample by construction. The gap between the in-sample Sharpe and the walk-forward Sharpe is the honest size of your overfit. Large gap means curve-fit. If the walk-forward holds across many refits, you have something closer to real structure.
cards.depth: It surfaces regime fragility for free. If the model has to be re-tuned drastically every window to keep working, the parameters are noise dressed as signal. A strategy worth trading should stay roughly stable as the window rolls forward across different markets.

cards.hook: Recall it: +5% a flip, yet the path goes broke. Why?
cards.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="40" y1="200" x2="380" y2="200" stroke="#35302a"/><line x1="40" y1="30" x2="40" y2="200" stroke="#35302a"/><path d="M40 150 C 150 120, 260 95, 380 70" fill="none" stroke="#7fb4a2" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 150 C 150 165, 260 182, 380 193" fill="none" stroke="#d9a441" stroke-width="2"/><text x="210" y="58" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13">ensemble average (the crowd)</text><text x="165" y="215" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13">your single path over time</text><text x="46" y="26" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13">wealth</text></svg>
cards.body: Take the bet again: heads grows you 50%, tails shrinks you 40%. Across a crowd of gamblers measured at one instant the average is a tidy +5% a flip, so it looks free. Follow one gambler through time and the stake grinds to zero. The answer: **multiplicative gains and losses don't average, they compound**. A +50% then a -40% is 1.5 times 0.6, which is 0.9, a loss on every pair. The ensemble average and the time average are different numbers, and you only ever live one path, the time one.
cards.depth: This is ergodicity, and it is why sizing beats edge for survival. Every real trade is multiplicative on your capital, so the number that governs you is the time-average growth rate, not the expected value the crowd would collect standing side by side.

cards.hook: Full Kelly maximizes growth and still feels like ruin.
cards.body: Kelly sizing maximizes long-run geometric growth, but the growth-optimal bet endures gut-wrenching drawdowns. At full Kelly, a 50% peak-to-trough fall is routine, and you have roughly even odds of halving your stake before you double it. That is why survivors run **fractional Kelly**, typically a quarter to a half of the formula's output. They accept slightly slower compounding to make the ride survivable, because a strategy you abandon at the bottom of a drawdown has an effective growth rate of zero.
cards.depth: The math is why it works: at half-Kelly you keep about 75% of the maximum growth rate for half the volatility. Growth is quadratic near the optimum while risk is linear, so cutting size is cheap in return and expensive-saving in variance.

cards.hook: Music's AI suits attack the training set, not the songs.
cards.body: In June 2024 the major labels sued Suno and Udio, and the striking feature is how little the complaints argue that the outputs infringe. The theory is that copying millions of sound recordings to train the model is **itself the infringement**, whatever the model later produces. Both companies effectively conceded they trained on copyrighted recordings and leaned on fair use. That flips the usual music playbook, which fixates on output similarity in the 'Blurred Lines' mold, and puts the ingestion step on trial instead.
cards.depth: Why the stakes are existential: if training on recordings is not fair use, exposure is per-work statutory damages across a corpus of millions of tracks. That arithmetic, not any single output, is what reportedly pushed the posture toward licensing talks.

cards.hook: Praise seemed to hurt and scolding seemed to help. Neither did.
cards.body: Kahneman watched flight instructors conclude that praising a good landing produced a worse next one, and berating a bad landing produced a better one. Both patterns were **regression to the mean** and nothing else. An unusually good landing is partly luck, so the next is likely closer to average, meaning worse, no matter what you say. An unusually bad one is likely followed by better. The instructors were reading a statistical artifact as causation, and it taught them exactly the wrong lesson about how to treat people.
cards.depth: The same illusion runs through trading and management: a hot month regresses, a cold one regresses, and whatever you did in between gets the credit or the blame. Before crediting an intervention, ask what the extreme value would have done on its own.

cards.hook: Time blindness is a broken internal clock. Buy an external one.
cards.body: The deficit is not caring about deadlines, it is **feeling time pass**. Duration and elapsed time are estimated poorly, so a quick task silently eats an hour and a deadline stays abstract until it is on top of you. Willpower cannot fix a missing sense. The move is to externalize the clock: a visible analog countdown, a shrinking colored wedge rather than digits, turns elapsed time into something your eyes register continuously, the way a fuel gauge shows a tank draining. The urgency then comes from perception instead of a calculation your brain does not reliably run.
cards.depth: Why analog beats digital here: reading '1:47:00' requires you to compute what is left, an abstract step an under-aroused brain skips. A shrinking wedge is read pre-attentively, no arithmetic, which is the entire point.

cards.hook: Recall it: which connector between beats means a list, not a story?
cards.body: Read your beats aloud and listen to the seams between them. Give yourself a moment before the answer lands. It is **'and then.'** When scenes link with 'and then' they are merely adjacent, a pile of events with no engine. Trey Parker's fix: each beat should follow the last by 'but' (a reversal) or 'therefore' (a consequence). Those two words carry causation, and causation is what an ear feels as momentum. Every 'and then' in your outline is a seam to cut or rebuild.
cards.depth: Why it stays useful for you: audio fiction has no visuals to carry a slack scene, so a bored ear just wanders off. Mapping the connectors is a structural diagnostic you can run on a whole draft in minutes.

cards.hook: You get paid because fear costs more than it should.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="360" y2="200" stroke="#35302a" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="100" y="75" width="70" height="125" fill="#d9a441"/><rect x="230" y="110" width="70" height="90" fill="#7fb4a2"/><line x1="185" y1="75" x2="185" y2="110" stroke="#a89f8d" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 3"/><text x="192" y="96" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13">the premium</text><text x="112" y="218" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="14">Implied</text><text x="240" y="218" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="14">Realized</text><text x="60" y="55" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="14">Volatility, on average</text></svg>
cards.body: Options implied volatility sits **above the volatility that actually shows up**, on average, most of the time. That persistent gap is the variance risk premium: buyers overpay for protection and lottery upside, and sellers collect the difference as compensation for holding crash risk. It is not a mispricing you arbitrage away. It is a risk premium, so it pays steadily and then hands back a chunk in one violent stretch. Your job is sizing to survive the handback, not pretending the premium is free money.
cards.depth: The premium is largest in index options and richest when realized vol is calm, because that is exactly when the next gap-down is least priced in. Sell it graded to how stretched implied sits over trailing realized, not blindly.

cards.hook: Training on the books was fair use. Pirating them wasn't.
cards.body: In the 2025 Anthropic authors case, Judge Alsup drew a line most coverage blurred. Using lawfully obtained books to train a model was, in his words, **"exceedingly transformative"** and fair use. But downloading pirated copies to build a permanent internal library was a separate act of infringement, and that piece headed toward trial. The lesson for anyone building with data: how you train may be defensible while how you acquired the corpus is a distinct, un-transformed liability. Provenance of the inputs is its own lawsuit.
cards.depth: Anthropic reportedly settled the piracy exposure for around $1.5 billion in late 2025, before the library claim was tried. Fair-use training did not save it, because the settled claim was about sourcing, not learning. Two questions, two verdicts, two price tags.

cards.hook: Recall it: why did the fix for your worst month do nothing?
cards.body: You changed something right after a terrible stretch, and the next month was better. Feels causal. Usually it is **regression to the mean**: extreme outcomes are part luck, and luck does not repeat, so the next reading drifts back toward average whether you intervened or not. This is why bottom-tick tinkering with a trading system, a routine, or a diet keeps looking like genius. You test your changes at the exact moment the world was going to snap back on its own. Change things from a normal baseline, not a low.
cards.depth: The clean test is a control: would an unchanged version have recovered too? Without one, you are crediting the intervention for the mean doing its ordinary work. Trading systems and personal habits both fail this test constantly, and both punish you for over-fitting to a single bad patch.

cards.hook: Your brain runs on two tenses: now and not-now.
cards.body: A core ADHD mechanism is **time blindness**: the felt distance to a future event does not scale with the real clock. A deadline two weeks out and one two months out generate nearly the same non-urgency, until both collapse into now at the last moment. Willpower does not fix a perception gap. The move is to make time physical: an analog timer you can watch draining, a countdown on the wall, the task placed on a dated calendar block rather than held as "soon." You are not lazy about the future. You cannot feel it, so put it in front of your eyes.
cards.depth: This is why "I'll do it later" is honest, not evasive: later has no emotional weight to pull against now. Convert every "later" into a specific visible when, and the missing urgency gets borrowed from the clock instead of manufactured from guilt.

cards.hook: Your backtest didn't learn a strategy. It learned a decade.
cards.body: A rule that crushed 2010 to 2020 may have only learned **one macro regime**: zero rates, low vol, buy-the-dip reflexively rewarded. The edge was real inside that world and can vanish the moment the world changes, which is exactly when you have finally sized up into it. A backtest that spans a single regime is not evidence of a strategy. It is a photograph of one climate. Test across rate cycles, vol regimes, and at least one genuine crisis, and watch whether the edge survives the transitions or only the calm.
cards.depth: Walk-forward across regimes beats one long in-sample run: fit on one regime, test on the next, and demand the edge persist through the handoff. If performance clusters entirely in one macro backdrop, you have a regime bet wearing a strategy's clothes, and its worst drawdown is unsampled.

cards.hook: Implied volatility isn't a forecast. It's a price.
cards.body: Traders talk about implied vol as the crowd's prediction of future movement, but it is a risk-neutral quantity, not a real-world one. It is the number that makes an option's hedging cost break even under no-arbitrage pricing, and it bakes in a premium for whoever bears variance risk. That is why implied sits above realized on average, roughly 3-4 vol points on the index over long samples. You are not paid because the crowd forecasts badly. You are paid **to carry a risk the buyer wants off their book**, the same reason insurers earn a margin.
cards.depth: The gap is not free money. The same premium compensates for the fact that short-vol losses cluster in crashes, exactly when your other assets are falling too. Priced honestly, the edge is fair pay for correlated tail risk, not a mispricing waiting to be harvested.

cards.hook: Tennessee's voice law targets the tool, not just the use.
cards.body: The Midler line protects your voice from commercial misappropriation, so a non-commercial clone often slips through it. Tennessee's ELVIS Act (Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security Act, 2024) breaks that pattern. It makes a person's voice a property right and, unusually, creates liability for **distributing a tool whose primary function is unauthorized voice cloning**, whether or not any specific ad ever runs. That pushes the target upstream from the infringing output to the infringing instrument. Most publicity statutes never reach the toolmaker. Watch whether other states copy the tool-liability hook, because that is the part with real teeth.
cards.depth: The live risk is overbreadth. A general-purpose voice model has lawful uses, so 'primary purpose' litigation will decide whether the statute hits bad actors or sweeps in neutral technology, the same First Amendment fight playing out around nearly every AI-content law now.

cards.hook: Working memory fails, so put the next step where your eyes are.
cards.body: ADHD degrades working memory, the mental scratchpad that holds 'what I'm doing next' while you act. When it drops the thread, the task doesn't feel hard, it simply **vanishes from awareness** and something else fills the gap. The fix is not more willpower, it is moving the scratchpad outside your head: the next single action on a sticky at eye level, the file left open on screen, the tab you refuse to close. You are not organizing, you are compensating for a specific deficit. Externalize the one next step, not the whole plan, so re-entry costs nothing.
cards.depth: Whole to-do lists fail here because they store the plan, not the resumption point. What restores a dropped task is a cue for the very next physical move, sitting in the visual field you will actually return to. Cue the re-entry, not the intention.

cards.hook: Your backtest assumed your own orders don't move the price.
cards.body: Most backtests fill at the quoted price and stop there, but real orders eat liquidity and push the market against you, an effect that grows with size and shrinks with the stock's daily volume. A signal that looks great on $500k can be worthless at $50M because **your own trading becomes the cost**. Impact roughly scales with the square root of your order as a fraction of daily volume, so ten times the size is not ten times the cost, it is more. Capacity, not raw edge, decides whether a strategy survives contact with real money.
cards.depth: This is why published anomalies fade after publication and why funds cap AUM per strategy. Test it by re-running with a size-dependent slippage model and asking at what dollar size the edge goes to zero. That number is the strategy's real ceiling, and it is usually lower than you hope.

cards.hook: Overconfidence has three faces. Which one quietly kills a trader?
cards.body: A few days back: Moore and Healy split overconfidence into three things that don't move together. Take a beat before the answer. Overestimation is thinking you did better than you did. Overplacement is thinking you beat other people. And the third, the one that wrecks position sizing, is **overprecision**, believing your range of outcomes is narrower than it really is. It is the quiet killer because you can be perfectly unbiased about direction and still bet as if the future were certain. Not wrong about the call, wrong about the width of the call.
cards.depth: Worth re-filing because the other two feel like ego and get caught in the mirror. Overprecision hides inside your risk model as confidence intervals that are simply too tight, so it surfaces as oversized positions and blown stops, never as an obvious mistake you can point to.

cards.hook: Dealers short gamma make the market move more.
cards.body: When market makers are net short gamma, staying hedged forces them to **sell as prices fall and buy as prices rise**, feeding the move they are chasing. When they are net long gamma the reverse holds: they buy dips and sell rips, and realized volatility gets pinned down. Around large option expiries the sign of that positioning can flip, which is why a quiet, mean-reverting tape turns into an air pocket with no headline behind it. The flows are mechanical, not discretionary, so they persist until the exposure rolls off.
cards.depth: The effect scales with how much open interest sits near spot and how close expiration is, since gamma concentrates there. Dealer positioning is inferred, never published, so treat any single 'gamma flip level' as a reported estimate rather than a fact you can lean on.

cards.hook: The first AI training ruling rejected fair use.
cards.body: In early 2025 a federal court in Thomson Reuters v. Ross Intelligence granted summary judgment against a fair-use defense for copying Westlaw headnotes to train a legal-research tool. Practitioners citing it as the answer to the generative cases are **overreading a narrow holding**: Ross built a non-generative search product, and the court expressly said its reasoning might come out differently for generative models. The output competed head-on with the source, which drove the market-harm analysis. It is a signal about direction, not a precedent that binds the Stability or OpenAI fights.
cards.depth: The fourth fair-use factor, effect on the market, did the work here because Ross was building a Westlaw substitute. Generative defendants argue their output does not replace any single training input, which is exactly the question the Ross court declined to reach.

cards.hook: Positive expected value can still ruin everyone who takes it.
cards.body: The trap is averaging across people instead of across time. Flip a coin: heads grows your stake 50%, tails shrinks it 40%. The **ensemble average is +5% per flip** measured across many gamblers, so it looks like free money. But follow one gambler through repeated flips and the path grinds toward zero, because 1.5 times 0.6 equals 0.9, a loss on every pair. What enriches a crowd measured at one instant bankrupts an individual measured over time. That gap is why position sizing, not edge, decides survival.
cards.depth: The ensemble average imagines many parallel gamblers and sums their outcomes; the time average follows one gambler down one road. They only agree when a process is 'ergodic,' and multiplicative bets are not. That is the mathematical spine underneath the Kelly criterion.

cards.hook: Don't make the reward bigger. Make it sooner.
cards.body: An ADHD brain discounts delayed rewards far more steeply than a neurotypical one, so a payoff months out barely moves the needle no matter how large it is. Trying to self-motivate by inflating the stakes ('this deal is worth six figures') fails, because the size lives in the future and the future is nearly invisible. The move is to **manufacture an immediate consequence**: a deadline today, a visible tally, money on the line this week. You are not weak-willed about the big goal. You are correctly responding to a reward your neurology cannot feel yet.
cards.depth: This is temporal discounting, one of the more replicated behavioral findings in ADHD. It is also why body doubling and hard deadlines work when willpower does not: both drag the consequence into the present, where your reward system can actually register it.

cards.hook: Your backtest filled at the midpoint. You won't.
cards.body: Most backtests price every entry and exit at the quoted mid, but you cross the spread each time you trade, and on options that spread is brutal. A strategy netting four cents of theoretical edge per contract can be entirely eaten by a five-cent-wide market before you count commissions or slippage into a moving book. **Half the round-trip spread times the number of trades** is the tax the backtest silently omits. The more a strategy trades, the more of its paper edge is imaginary, which is where high-turnover systems quietly die.
cards.depth: A fast sanity check: rerun the backtest filling at the bid on buys and the ask on sells, then again at mid, and compare. If the edge survives the pessimistic fill it is real. If it only exists at the mid, you found a market-maker's profit, not yours.

cards.hook: A covered call is a short put in disguise.
cards.body: Put-call parity is not abstract. Long stock plus a short call at strike K equals, in payoff and risk, a short put at K. Your 'conservative' buy-write is **synthetically a short put**: same capped upside, same downside all the way to zero, same short-volatility exposure. The income-strategy branding hides that you are running the identical position a cash-secured put seller runs, just with more capital tied up and worse assignment and tax mechanics. If you would flinch at naked-putting the name, you should flinch at buy-writing it.
cards.depth: Practical tell: the two have the same delta, gamma, vega and theta at every point. Choose between them on capital efficiency, borrow, dividends and tax treatment, not on how safe the label happens to sound.

cards.hook: Make the checker a different call than the writer.
cards.body: Generation and verification are asymmetric: spotting a flaw in a finished answer is cheaper and more reliable than producing that answer was. A model grading its own output in the same context inherits its own blind spots, so it rubber-stamps. Spin up a **separate verifier call** with a narrow, adversarial instruction, find the error, assume one exists, and it catches mistakes the author structurally cannot see. This is why fresh-eyes review works for humans, and why single-agent self-critique so often just confirms the first draft instead of breaking it.
cards.depth: Design move: give the verifier a different job than 'is this good?' Ask it to locate the specific wrong line or produce the failing case. Judging invites agreement; locating forces it to actually go look.

cards.hook: In 1948 the studios were ordered to sell their theaters.
cards.body: The Paramount antitrust decrees forced the major studios to divest their theater chains and banned **block booking**, the practice of making exhibitors buy films in bundles, sight unseen, to get the ones they actually wanted. This broke the vertical integration that had powered the studio system since the 1920s, made room for independents and television, and shaped how films were sold for decades. A court terminated the decrees in 2020, right as streaming was rebuilding the same vertical control the ruling had spent 72 years dismantling.
cards.depth: The rhyme worth noting: bundling never died, it moved. Block booking sold theaters a slate they couldn't unbundle. A streaming subscription sells viewers a catalog they can't unbundle either. Same economics, new pipe.

cards.hook: Disagree on the forecast? Don't split it. Bet it.
cards.body: Two sides stuck on what a business will earn usually compromise on one number, which guarantees both are wrong and someone feels robbed. The sharper move is a **contingent structure**: an earnout, a contingent value right, a backend tied to the actual result. Each side is effectively paid if its own forecast proves right, so the fight over one number becomes a bet each is happy to take. It also flushes out bluffing, because whoever refuses to tie price to results was quietly inflating the projection.
cards.depth: Caveat: contingent terms move the fight to measurement. Define the metric, the audit right, and anti-manipulation covenants up front, because whoever controls the books after close controls the payout. A clean earnout is mostly good definitions.

cards.hook: Recall it: is your bias or your scatter the bigger error?
cards.body: Take a beat before the answer lands. Measure a set of judges, forecasters, or underwriters on identical cases and you find two errors, not one. Bias is the shared tilt off target. The other is how much they disagree with each other, and Kahneman's work found it contributes **as much total error as bias**, often more. That's noise, and you cannot feel it from inside a single judgment. So the underrated fix is not debiasing yourself. It's averaging several independent estimates of the same thing.
cards.depth: Why it matters again: your own repeated calls are a noisy panel of one. Estimating the same trade or case twice, days apart, and averaging beats trusting today's single read, because today's read carries scatter you cannot detect.

cards.hook: A box spread is a loan wearing an options costume.
cards.body: Sell a bull call spread and a bear put spread at the same two strikes, and the payoff is fixed at the strike difference, guaranteed regardless of where the underlying lands. That fixed payoff makes the whole position a **synthetic zero-coupon bond**. Sell the box and you have borrowed cash today against a fixed repayment at expiry. Buy it and you have lent. On European, cash-settled index options like SPX there is no early assignment to wreck it, so the implied rate often lands within a few basis points of Treasury bill yields, and it clears as Section 1256.
cards.depth: The rate is only clean if the options are genuinely European and cash-settled. Run the same trade on American-style single-stock options and early exercise can convert your neat loan into an assignment you never wanted. That is why practitioners build boxes on SPX, not on Apple.

cards.hook: Interest is the fuel, so bolt boring tasks to it.
cards.body: An ADHD brain responds weakly to rewards that are small, distant, or abstract, which describes most admin work. Willpower does not fix a fuel problem. The concrete move is **temptation bundling**: only let yourself have a strong immediate reward while the dull task is running. The podcast you love plays only while you clear the inbox. The good coffee gets made only at the desk where the filing waits. You are not disciplining the boring task, you are lending it the salience it lacks by chaining it to something your brain already wants right now.
cards.depth: Wharton's Katherine Milkman tested this by letting subjects hear addictive audiobooks only at the gym, and attendance rose. The ADHD version bites harder because the reward gap it fills is bigger. One rule keeps it working: the treat is exclusive to the task, or the bundle quietly unravels.

cards.hook: When a measure becomes a target, it stops measuring.
cards.body: This is **Goodhart's Law**, and it explains why your cleanest metric rots the moment you optimize it. The mechanism: any proxy captures the real goal imperfectly, leaving slack between the two. Push hard on the proxy and effort pours into that slack, tightening the link between your action and the metric while loosening the link between the metric and the goal. A strategy tuned to maximize backtest Sharpe learns the noise. A billable-hours target grows hours, not value. The number keeps climbing and tells you less each time.
cards.depth: Marilyn Strathern coined the modern wording. Charles Goodhart's original was about monetary aggregates that misbehaved the instant central banks targeted them. Same shape everywhere: the map you steer by is the first map your steering redraws.

cards.hook: California now protects dead performers from AI resurrection.
cards.body: **AB 1836**, effective January 2025, bars using a digital replica of a deceased performer in films, shows, or sound recordings without consent from the estate. It amended the existing postmortem right of publicity, so the newsworthy part is not that the dead have rights, they already did, but that "digital replica" is now named explicitly and the default flips to consent. Where practitioners overread it: the exemptions track classic publicity defenses. News, public affairs, documentary, satire, comment, and a fleeting or incidental use are all carved out.
cards.depth: Its sibling, AB 2602, governs the living: a contract letting a studio make a digital replica is unenforceable if the use is not specifically described and the performer lacked union or legal representation. Two statutes, one theme, consent must be particular, not buried in boilerplate.

cards.hook: Replace 'and then' with 'but' or 'therefore'.
cards.body: Trey Parker's test for whether a story has an engine: read your beats aloud and listen to the connective word between them. If scenes link with **"and then," you have a list, not a story**. The events are merely adjacent. When each beat instead follows from the last by "but" (a reversal) or "therefore" (a consequence), you have causation, and causation is what a listener feels as momentum. For audio fiction especially, where a bored ear just wanders off, this is a fast diagnostic: map the connectors, and every "and then" is a seam to cut or rebuild.
cards.depth: The rule scales up. The same but/therefore chain that binds two beats should bind two acts. A midpoint that merely happens after the setup is an "and then" at structural scale, and it sags in exactly the same way a limp scene does.

cards.hook: At-the-money time value shrinks with the square root of time left.
cards.body: An at-the-money option's extrinsic value scales roughly with sigma times the square root of time, not time itself. So cutting the calendar from 30 days to 15 does not halve the premium; it removes only about 29% of it. The other side of that curve is brutal: because value tracks the square root of time, **theta accelerates as expiry approaches**, and the daily bleed goes near-vertical in the last few sessions. Front-week premium looks cheap in dollars precisely because most of its decay is still ahead of it.
cards.depth: This is why selling the final week harvests decay fastest but hands you the ugliest gamma, and why a calendar spread earns its keep from the back month decaying slowly while the front collapses. The convexity is the trade, both directions.

cards.hook: A vague AI-replica clause is unenforceable unless the performer had counsel.
cards.body: California AB 2602, effective January 1 2025, added a consent test with teeth. A contract provision letting a producer create or use a digital replica of a performer is unenforceable if two things are both true: it lacks a **reasonably specific description of the intended uses**, and the performer was not represented by legal counsel or a union rep who negotiated on their behalf. The old all-purpose likeness grant, drafted broad on purpose, now fails on its own vagueness. Specificity plus representation is the enforceability gate, not the length of the release.
cards.depth: It rhymes with the SAG-AFTRA specificity standard but reaches non-union deals too, which is where the exposure concentrates. For a producer the practical move is to describe uses narrowly and document representation, because a blanket grant you cannot enforce is worse than a tailored one you can.

cards.hook: Pre-decide the trigger, not the goal, and the task starts itself.
cards.body: Initiation off a general intention ("I'll do the deal memo today") leans on executive function, which is the weak link. An if-then plan, "when I sit down with coffee, I open the memo," binds the action to a specific perceptual cue instead. Now starting runs off **perception, not willpower**: the environment triggers the behavior the way a smell triggers a memory, with the effortful decision already spent in advance. Gollwitzer's implementation-intentions research shows the effect is largest exactly where self-regulation is hardest, which is the ADHD case.
cards.depth: The craft detail: the cue must be concrete and already in your day (a time, a place, a preceding action you always do), not a vague state like "when I feel ready." A cue you never actually encounter fires never. Wire the trigger to something that already happens.

cards.hook: Adding a detail makes a story likelier to believe and likelier wrong.
cards.body: Every extra condition you attach to a forecast can only lower its true joint probability, since a conjunction is at most as likely as its least likely part. Yet added specifics make the scenario feel more plausible, because the mind scores it on how representative it seems, not on the math. That is the **conjunction fallacy**, the Linda problem in Kahneman and Tversky's work. A rich, detailed narrative forecast reads as more convincing and is statistically the weaker bet.
cards.depth: It matters at work directly: a vivid pitch ("rates cut, then a rotation into small caps, then a Q3 melt-up") sells better and is less likely than any single leg of it. When a story gains persuasiveness by gaining specifics, treat that as a warning, not a confirmation.

cards.hook: Recall it: how did a correct oil hedge still cause bankruptcy?
cards.body: Metallgesellschaft, early 1990s, had sold long-dated fixed-price oil delivery contracts and hedged with a rolling stack of near-month futures. Price risk: covered. Take a beat before the answer. Then oil fell, and the trap sprang on timing, not direction. The futures threw off **immediate cash margin calls**, while the offsetting gains on the delivery contracts would not be realized for years. Right on price, fatal on cash flow. Reported loss around $1.3 billion, from a hedge that was directionally sound the whole way down.
cards.depth: Why it matters again: any hedge that marks one leg to market in cash while the other accrues over time carries funding risk that is fully separate from price risk. The position can be correct and still die because you run out of cash to hold it. Match the cash-flow timing, not just the direction.

cards.hook: You can't own positive theta and positive gamma at once.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><line x1="40" y1="120" x2="360" y2="120" stroke="#35302a"/><text x="200" y="20" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">Theta and gamma always oppose</text><rect x="80" y="70" width="28" height="50" fill="#d9a441"/><rect x="118" y="120" width="28" height="45" fill="#7fb4a2"/><text x="113" y="185" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">Long gamma</text><rect x="250" y="120" width="28" height="50" fill="#d9a441"/><rect x="288" y="75" width="28" height="45" fill="#7fb4a2"/><text x="283" y="200" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">Short gamma</text><text x="360" y="80" fill="#d9a441" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="end">gamma</text><text x="360" y="160" fill="#7fb4a2" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="end">theta</text></svg>
cards.body: For a delta-hedged option, theta and gamma carry **opposite signs by construction**: theta is roughly minus one-half times gamma times price-squared times variance. So owning convexity (long gamma) means paying time decay every day, and being short gamma means collecting theta as your fee for the risk. There is no configuration where both help you. The whole options trade reduces to one question: is the premium you collect for negative gamma larger than the realized moves that gamma will cost you? That gap is the variance premium wearing a different hat.
cards.depth: Practical read: theta is the price tag on gamma, not a separate income stream. A short strangle that shows fat daily theta is not a yield machine. It is you being paid, correctly or not, to absorb the gamma losses of the next big move.

cards.hook: Denmark wants to give you copyright in your own face.
cards.body: Instead of a standalone publicity right, Denmark's government proposed (reported 2025) amending copyright law so every person **owns the copyright in their own facial features, voice, and body**. The point is leverage: publicity rights vary by jurisdiction and often die with the person, but copyright ships with fast notice-and-takedown machinery and statutory damages. Graft identity onto copyright and a deepfake becomes infringement you can pull down like a pirated film. The odd part is conceptual, since copyright protects authored works and not who you happen to be, and other EU states are watching whether it holds up.
cards.depth: Why a practitioner should care: this borrows a takedown regime that already scales globally through platform copyright tooling, rather than building deepfake enforcement from scratch. If it survives drafting, expect it cited as a template well outside Denmark.

cards.hook: Background noise can raise focus in an under-aroused brain.
cards.body: The moderate-brain-arousal model holds that ADHD prefrontal circuits often **run under-aroused**, so a dull low-stimulation task drops arousal below the level attention needs to lock on. Adding one controlled stimulation channel, such as instrumental music, white noise, gum, or pacing, nudges arousal back toward the useful range, which is why fidgeting frequently sharpens concentration instead of breaking it. The move: for a boring task, deliberately add a stimulation source rather than chasing a silent room, and reserve silence for work that is already engaging on its own. Treat it as a lever to pull, not a quirk to apologize for.
cards.depth: Related idea, stochastic resonance: a small amount of noise can help a weak signal cross a detection threshold. Reported findings suggest noise aids attention more for inattentive profiles than for controls, which fits the under-arousal account rather than a one-size rule.

cards.hook: Overconfidence has three different faces, and they conflict.
cards.body: Moore and Healy showed overconfidence is not one trait but **three that often move in opposite directions**. Overestimation is thinking you scored better than you actually did. Overplacement is thinking you beat other people, the better-than-average effect. Overprecision is your confidence intervals being too narrow. On genuinely hard tasks people tend to underestimate their absolute performance yet still believe they outrank everyone, so two of the three fire at once pointing opposite ways. Lumping it all as overconfidence hides which one is biting you. For a trader, overprecision is the quiet killer: not being wrong, but sizing as if your range were certain.
cards.depth: Diagnostic value: ask which failure a given decision risks. A forecast bet is overprecision. A hiring-yourself-for-the-job call is overplacement. Different faces need different corrections, and the generic advice to be humble targets none of them.

cards.hook: Recall it: how does tomorrow's data leak into today's signal?
cards.body: Answer before reading on. Look-ahead bias is any input your backtest used that would not have been knowable at the moment of the trade: restated earnings shown at their final value, index membership assigned retroactively, or trading at a closing price you only learned at that close. The tell is an equity curve that looks too clean and falls apart the instant you lag every input by one bar. The fix is **point-in-time data**: stamp each value by when it was actually available, not the date it describes, and act only on what a live system could have seen.
cards.depth: It is the most seductive bug because it flatters you. Survivorship and multiple-testing bias inflate results; look-ahead often makes them look nearly perfect, which is exactly when you should get suspicious rather than excited.

cards.hook: Gamma decides where your implied-versus-realized edge actually lands.
cards.body: A delta-hedged short option earns, each day, roughly half its gamma times the square of the underlying, multiplied by the gap between implied and realized variance. So you never collect the volatility premium evenly. You collect it **weighted by gamma**, which is largest at-the-money and in the final days. Almost all of your realized edge accrues when price sits near your strike late in the trade. You can be right on vol over the whole life and still lose, because the big moves arrived exactly where your gamma was highest.
cards.depth: This is why 'implied looks rich, so sell it' is not enough. Two paths with identical total realized volatility can hand you opposite results depending on when the moves came relative to your gamma. Entry vol edge sets the odds; the path decides the payout.

cards.hook: Voice-rights law only bites when the clone sells something.
cards.body: The right of publicity, the line running from Bette Midler's 1988 win against Ford, protects your voice from commercial misappropriation: an ad, a fake endorsement. But a synthetic song, a deepfaked interview, or a non-commercial parody often slips that frame. And there is **no federal right of publicity**, so a clone that is legal in one state can be actionable in another. That patchwork, not anything technically new about AI, is the real hole. It is why states keep passing voice statutes and why a national floor keeps getting proposed.
cards.depth: Practitioner error: assuming Midler-style claims cover AI voice broadly. They are limited to commercial-use contexts and vary wildly by state, from robust post-mortem rights in California to none elsewhere. The AI-specific statutes exist to fill exactly that commercial-use-plus-no-national-standard gap, not because old doctrine failed on the technology.

cards.hook: Bias is your aim. Noise is your scatter, and it's bigger.
cards.body: Measure a group of judges, underwriters, or forecasters on the same cases and you find two errors, not one. Bias is the shared tilt off target. Noise is how much they disagree with each other. Kahneman's work found that noise contributes as much total error as bias, sometimes more, and you cannot feel it from inside a single judgment. Debiasing gets all the attention. The cheaper fix is often to cut the scatter: use structure, checklists, or **average several independent estimates** of the same thing.
cards.depth: Averaging independent judgments works because their random errors partly cancel, shrinking variance without anyone becoming less biased. It is the same math as wisdom of crowds. One caveat: the estimates must be genuinely independent. Let people talk first and they converge on a shared error, which trades noise for more bias.

cards.hook: More medication stops helping long before its side effects stop.
cards.body: Stimulant benefit follows a dose-response curve that flattens out. Past a moderate dose, extra symptom relief gets small fast. The physical costs, higher heart rate, killed appetite, wrecked sleep, keep rising in a roughly straight line. So the target is not the highest dose you can tolerate. It is the **minimum effective dose**, the lowest amount that clearly works. Chasing 'more focus' upward tends to buy a flatter, more wired version of the same result you already had, at a worse price.
cards.depth: Concrete move for a titration: change one variable at a time and give each level one to two weeks, judged on real output and side effects, not on how it feels day three. The felt novelty of a new dose fades; the steady-state effect is what you are actually buying.

cards.hook: Recall it: why does testing 200 strategies fake a winner?
cards.body: Because chance alone produces impressive backtests when you run enough of them. Test 200 unrelated strategies and several will post a high Sharpe on luck. Then you pick the best one, which means you **selected for being lucky, not for being good**. That is multiple-testing bias. The defense is to haircut the result by how hard you searched, using an out-of-sample check or a deflated Sharpe that discounts for the number of trials. The more variants you tried, the bigger the discount your winner deserves.
cards.depth: A quick gut check before you trust any backtest: ask how many variants were tried and quietly discarded to reach this one. That hidden count, far more than the equity curve, sets how much you should trust the Sharpe. A curve found on the first try means something a curve found on the two-hundredth does not.

cards.hook: You're not selling volatility on the index. You're selling correlation.
cards.body: Index variance decomposes into single-name variance plus the correlations between the names. When you sell index options, most of the premium above the weighted single-name vol is a **correlation risk premium**: the market pays up for index puts because in a crash everything moves together and diversification vanishes exactly when you need it. That is why index implied vol usually trades richer than the implied vol of its components, and why dispersion traders sell index vol and buy single-name vol. You are short the thing that spikes toward one in a panic.
cards.depth: The catch: implied correlation is bounded near one, so you are short a variable with a hard ceiling and a soft floor. It pays steadily while names stay differentiated and loses violently when correlation jumps toward one in a selloff. Same shape as every short-vol trade, one layer down.

cards.hook: Training liability and output liability are two different lawsuits.
cards.body: Most AI-rights confusion collapses two separate questions. The **input question** is whether ingesting copyrighted works to train a model infringes, which is where fair use gets fought. The output question is whether a specific generation copies protected expression, which is ordinary substantial-similarity analysis with no training defense attached. A model can be trained lawfully and still produce an infringing frame, or trained unlawfully and produce something wholly original. When you paper an AI-assisted production, you need reps and indemnities covering both, because a clean training pedigree does not immunize a single infringing output.
cards.depth: This is why chain-of-title diligence on generative tools is two-layered: what was the model trained on, and what safeguards catch infringing outputs. The Anthropic and Meta rulings largely addressed inputs; output liability is still litigated case by case under classic copying rules.

cards.hook: Your best productivity system will quietly stop working in weeks.
cards.body: ADHD attention is captured by novelty, so a new tool or routine delivers a burst of dopamine that carries you through the friction of using it. When the novelty fades, so does the pull, and the system goes invisible: still on your desk, no longer seen. This is **tool decay**, and treating it as a personal failure is the error. The move is to expect it. Build a small rotation of two or three equivalent systems and swap when one goes dead, rather than hunting for the one permanent tool that does not exist.
cards.depth: Corollary: judge a system by how it fails, not how it starts. Everything works in week one on novelty alone. The ones worth keeping are the ones you can restart cheaply after you inevitably drop them, because you will drop them.

cards.hook: Your winning strategy was tested only on the companies that survived.
cards.body: Standard price databases quietly drop companies that went bankrupt, delisted, or were acquired at a loss. Backtest on today's index membership and you have unknowingly filtered your universe to **the winners that made it**, which inflates returns and hides exactly the tail risk the strategy would have eaten. The effect is largest for anything that buys beaten-down or distressed names, because those are the ones most likely to have vanished from the data. Fix it with a point-in-time universe that includes every ticker as it existed then, dead ones included.
cards.depth: Reported magnitudes vary, but survivorship-clean studies routinely knock a meaningful chunk off long-only equity backtests, and more off small-cap and deep-value tilts. If your data vendor cannot tell you when a ticker died, assume it silently deleted it.

cards.hook: Recall it: what makes splitting each issue 50/50 the worst outcome?
cards.body: When two sides rank the open issues differently, meeting in the middle on every one leaves joint value unclaimed. The better move is to trade across issues instead: give the cheap-to-you point to win the expensive-to-them one. That is **logrolling**, and bundling is how you find it. 'You take the credit and the announce date; I take the audit right and the reversion.' Single-issue haggling can never surface those trades, because it never lets either side reveal what it actually cares about.
cards.depth: Every deal with more than one term is a chance to logroll, but only if you keep issues open at once instead of closing them one by one. Sequential haggling locks in 50/50 splits before either side learns the other's ranking. Keep a live issues list and settle it as a package.

cards.hook: VIX futures usually cost more the longer you wait.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="50" y1="200" x2="370" y2="200" stroke="#35302a" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="50" y1="200" x2="50" y2="30" stroke="#35302a" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="210" y="228" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">time to expiry</text><text x="20" y="120" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" transform="rotate(-90 20 120)" text-anchor="middle">price</text><polyline points="62,168 140,128 220,104 300,90 360,82" fill="none" stroke="#d9a441" stroke-width="2.5"/><line x1="50" y1="168" x2="360" y2="168" stroke="#7fb4a2" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="4 4"/><text x="356" y="162" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="end">spot</text><text x="120" y="64" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="14">contango: later = pricier</text><text x="150" y="150" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13">held future rolls down, bleeds</text></svg>
cards.body: In calm regimes the VIX term structure sits in **contango**: each further-out future prices above spot. A long-vol position holding those futures loses a little every day as each one rolls down toward a lower spot, whether or not volatility ever rises. Reported figures put VIX futures in contango roughly 75 to 85% of trading days. That roll cost is why buy-and-hold VIX products decay toward zero, and why long vol is a timing trade, not a hold.
cards.depth: The mirror image is backwardation in a panic, when near-term fear prices above the curve and the roll pays you instead. So the same structure that bleeds in calm markets pays in a crash. Sizing long vol means budgeting the daily roll as an insurance premium you are paying, not treating a flat tape as a free hold.

cards.hook: The next AI-training fight is about dilution, not copying.
cards.body: In the 2025 training cases, courts leaned toward calling the copying itself transformative. What tripped plaintiffs up was the fourth fair-use factor, market harm. A federal judge in a 2025 Meta case suggested the strongest theory is **market dilution**: not that the model copied your book, but that its cheap synthetic substitutes flood and depress the market you sell into. The copying got waved through; the live question is whether a model trained on you can then compete you out of existence.
cards.depth: This flips litigation strategy. Plaintiffs need evidence of a real substitution market, foreclosed licensing, or measurable price erosion, not just proof their work sat in the training set. Defendants win by showing outputs do not compete in the same market. Discovery shifts from what did you ingest to what does your output displace.

cards.hook: After the fact, you'll swear you saw it coming.
cards.body: Once you know the outcome, memory quietly rewrites your earlier estimate to look smarter, an effect called **hindsight bias**. A 40% call becomes 'I basically knew it.' The damage is not vanity. It is that you can never learn calibration from a memory that edits itself, because every past forecast now feels well-judged. The only defense is a timestamped record of what you actually predicted, made before the result existed to contaminate it.
cards.depth: This is why a written prediction log beats honest reflection. It also explains why post-mortems blame people: once the failure is known, the warning signs look obvious and someone should have caught them. They were not obvious inside the decision. Judge the process against what was knowable then, not against what you know now.

cards.hook: Your ADHD med is inert until your blood cuts it apart.
cards.body: Lisdexamfetamine is dexamphetamine bolted to the amino acid lysine, and it does nothing until enzymes in your red blood cells cleave that lysine off. The conversion is **rate-limited by your blood, not a pill coating**, which is why onset is gradual and the tail is even. Two consequences follow: dose it early, because it ramps slowly and you want it working by morning, and do not bother splitting or crushing it, because the bottleneck is enzymatic, not the capsule.
cards.depth: The same enzymatic gate is why the dose-response is steadier from person to person and why the drug is harder to misuse. It also means a 'barely noticeable' read in the first days is expected, not failure. Judge titration over weeks, at a fixed daily time, never by the verdict of one morning.

cards.hook: Recall it: which shorts in your backtest could never be borrowed?
cards.body: The winners a long-short backtest loves are often the hardest-to-borrow names: small, distressed, heavily shorted, exactly the stocks a broker will not lend you or will lend only at punishing fees. Your backtest assumes free, unlimited borrow. **The edge lived in trades you could never actually place.** The fix is to filter your short universe to liquid, borrowable names, or subtract realistic borrow costs, then see how much alpha was a lending fantasy.
cards.depth: The same illusion appears on the long side as capacity: a signal that prints on micro-caps evaporates once your size moves the price. Both are execution ceilings the backtest silently ignores. A returns curve is only as real as the trades beneath it were fillable at the prices it assumed.

cards.hook: The option smile leans because crashes cluster and rallies don't.
cards.body: Equity index puts trade at higher implied vol than equidistant calls. Retail calls it fear pricing, and fear is part of it. The deeper reason is that index returns are genuinely negatively skewed. Big down days arrive with volatility spikes and correlations racing toward one, while rallies grind slowly. So downside strikes really do sit on more variance, and sellers price that asymmetry in. **The skew is a forecast of the return distribution's shape, not just a sentiment tax.** Treat a flattening skew as the market repricing crash odds, not as free premium.
cards.depth: Mechanically, the leverage effect and forced deleveraging make volatility itself rise when prices fall, so a put hedges two things at once, direction and the vol spike that rides along with it. That double duty is what a call the same distance away cannot offer, and it is why the smirk rarely vanishes in a healthy equity index.

cards.hook: SAG-AFTRA splits digital replicas in two, and consent must be specific.
cards.body: The 2023 TV and theatrical contract drew a line practitioners still blur. An employment-based digital replica is built from a performer's work during their engagement. An independently created one is made outside it, from other material. Both require the performer's clear consent and separate pay, and that consent has to carry a **reasonably specific description of the intended use**. A buried, all-purpose grant does not cut it. So the drafting question is no longer whether you can make a replica, but whether your consent language survives that specificity test.
cards.depth: This is why studio AI riders now read like scope-of-license clauses. They enumerate mediums, projects, and duration rather than granting replica rights at large. The parallel for any deal lawyer is right-of-publicity licensing, where a vague grant has always been construed against the drafter. Specificity is not caution here, it is the enforceability requirement.

cards.hook: The fix worked because you tried it at rock bottom.
cards.body: Any extreme reading is part signal and part luck. When you act at the worst moment, the next measurement drifts back toward your true average on its own, and your intervention takes the credit. This is **regression to the mean**, and it fakes cause and effect everywhere. Kahneman watched flight instructors conclude that scolding a bad landing helped and praising a great one backfired. Both were just regression. A terrible landing was likely to be followed by a better one regardless, and a superb one by a worse one. Distrust any before-and-after that started at an extreme.
cards.depth: The trading version is obvious once you see it. A system tweaked right after its worst drawdown usually rebounds, and the tweak looks brilliant. Run the counterfactual. Would the untouched system have recovered anyway? Often yes. The only clean test is a control, a comparison to what the same starting point does when you change nothing at all.

cards.hook: A perfect oil hedge went bankrupt on its own margin calls.
cards.body: In the early 1990s a Metallgesellschaft unit sold long-dated fixed-price contracts to deliver oil for years, then hedged by holding a stack of near-month futures it kept rolling forward. On paper the price risk was covered. Then oil fell. The futures threw off immediate margin calls in cash, while the offsetting gains on the delivery contracts would not arrive until far in the future. The hedge was directionally sound and still nearly sank the company, reportedly around a $1.3 billion loss. **A hedge that is right on price can still kill you on timing.**
cards.depth: The second wound was the term structure. The stack-and-roll earned money while the market stayed in backwardation, but the curve flipped to contango and every roll began to bleed. A cash-flow mismatch plus an adverse roll is the same pair that shows up in levered ETFs and futures carry today. Being right about the destination does not pay the calls you owe along the way.

cards.hook: Recall it: what does an ADHD brain fail to feel, not fight?
cards.body: Take a beat before the answer lands. The deficit is not laziness or thin discipline. It is **interval timing**, the internal sense of how much time has actually gone by. Duration does not register, so a five-minute email eats an hour and a deadline three days out feels unreal. That is why trying harder does nothing. You cannot muscle a sense you do not have. The move is a prosthetic that puts time into your visual field, an analog timer with a shrinking wedge, a countdown on a second screen, a clock you actually glance at.
cards.depth: Retrieving this again matters because the failure keeps returning in fresh disguises. A build that runs long, a bedtime that slips, a call that overruns. Same missing gauge each time. Adding a timer does not train you to track time, it converts an invisible quantity into something the eyes can see and the broken internal clock cannot quietly hide.

cards.hook: A fat dividend can get your short call assigned early.
cards.body: American-style short calls face early exercise risk when a call's extrinsic value drops below the dividend the stock is about to pay. A holder who exercises the night before ex-date captures the dividend and forfeits only the now-cheap time value. It's not random: it clusters right before ex-dividend dates on deep ITM, low-IV calls. Assignment lands you short stock at the open, **owing the dividend to whoever exercised**. Check ex-div calendars before holding short calls into dividend-heavy names.
cards.depth: Deep ITM covered calls on dividend aristocrats are the classic trap: sell a call worth $0.50 of extrinsic value against a $0.60 dividend and assignment is nearly certain. Brokers don't warn you; you find out via an overnight position change. It's also why call open interest on dividend stocks drops sharply right before ex-date, as short sellers who understand the math close out first.

cards.hook: Only two levers reliably open your starting gate.
cards.body: ADHD task initiation runs on an interest-based nervous system, not an importance-based one. Deadlines and stakes don't reliably trigger the dopamine needed to start; **novelty and urgency do**. That's why a task due in three weeks sits untouched, then gets finished in the last two hours. The three-week version has no urgency signal yet. Manufacture one: fake deadlines, timers, public commitments, or breaking work into a five-minute first step reframes 'important' into something your brain will act on now.
cards.depth: This isn't a willpower gap, it's a difference in what counts as a starting signal. Importance gets evaluated consciously; urgency and novelty trigger dopamine more directly and involuntarily. Body doubling and hard deadlines work for the same reason: they import urgency from outside instead of waiting for it to build on its own.

cards.hook: Outside view beats inside view for time estimates.
cards.body: The inside view estimates a task by reasoning through its specific steps: what has to happen, in what order, how long each piece takes. It reliably underestimates, because it can't account for what you haven't anticipated yet. The **outside view** asks a different question: how long did similar projects actually take, ignoring this one's details. Kahneman calls this reference-class forecasting. It's uncomfortable because it throws away information that feels relevant, and accurate because that's exactly what makes every planner overconfident.
cards.depth: Flyvbjerg's research on infrastructure megaprojects found this pattern at scale: planners reasoning from their own project's specifics were consistently more wrong than planners who simply asked what similar projects historically took. The fix isn't sharper inside reasoning, it's finding your reference class first and anchoring there before you build the detailed estimate.
